title: Λύκος καὶ ἐρωδιός
part: The Wolf and the Heron (Chambry 224 · Perry 156)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 224 (= Perry 156). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Λύκος καταπιὼν ὀστοῦν περιῄει τὸν ἰασόμενον αὐτὸν ζητῶν.
sentences.tr: Lykos katapiōn ostoun periēiei ton iasomenon auton zētōn.
sentences.l: A wolf, having swallowed down a bone, was going about seeking the one who would heal him.
sentences.i: A wolf who had swallowed a bone went about looking for someone to cure him.
sentences.n: The future participle under the article, τὸν ἰασόμενον, names a person by what he is to do: 'the one who will heal him', which English turns into 'someone to heal him'. καταπίνω is to swallow straight down, whole.

sentences.t: Περιτυχὼν δὲ ἐρωδιῷ, τοῦτον παρεκάλει ἐπὶ μισθῷ τὸ ὀστοῦν ἐκβαλεῖν.
sentences.tr: Peritychōn de erōdiōi, touton parekalei epi misthōi to ostoun ekbalein.
sentences.l: And having fallen in with a heron, he kept calling on him to get the bone out for a fee.
sentences.n: περιτυγχάνω takes the dative of the person one falls in with. ἐπὶ μισθῷ — ἐπί with the dative naming the terms on which a thing is done. παρεκάλει is imperfect: he kept at him.

sentences.t: Κἀκεῖνος καθεὶς τὴν ἑαυτοῦ κεφαλὴν εἰς τὴν φάρυγγα αὐτοῦ τὸ ὀστοῦν ἐξέσπασε καὶ τὸν ὡμολογημένον μισθὸν ἀπῄτει.
sentences.tr: Kakeinos katheis tēn heautou kephalēn eis tēn pharynga autou to ostoun exespase kai ton hōmologēmenon misthon apēitei.
sentences.l: And that one, having let down his own head into his throat, drew the bone out and was demanding back the agreed fee.
sentences.i: And the heron let his own head down into the wolf's throat, drew the bone out, and asked back the fee agreed on.
sentences.n: Κἀκεῖνος is καὶ ἐκεῖνος run together by crasis. καθείς is the aorist participle of καθίημι, 'let down'. ὡμολογημένον is a perfect passive participle: the fee stands agreed, the bargain already struck and still binding. ἀπῄτει is 'was asking back', the imperfect of a man claiming what he already counts as his.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ὑποτυχὼν εἶπεν· « Ὦ οὗτος, οὐκ ἀγαπᾷς ἐκ λύκου στόματος σῴαν τὴν κεφαλὴν ἐξενεγκών, ἀλλὰ καὶ μισθὸν ἀπαιτεῖς ; »
sentences.tr: Ho de hypotychōn eipen· « Ō houtos, ouk agapāis ek lykou stomatos sōian tēn kephalēn exenenkōn, alla kai misthon apaiteis ; »
sentences.l: And he, taking-up-the-word, said: « You there, are you not content, having brought your head out safe from a wolf's mouth, but demand a fee besides? »
sentences.i: And the wolf took up the word and said: « You there — are you not satisfied to have got your head out of a wolf's mouth whole, that you must ask a fee on top of it? »
sentences.n: ὑποτυχών is the house word for taking up the word in reply, not for any physical seizing. Ὦ οὗτος is a rough way of hailing a man, near to 'hey, you'. ἀγαπάω here is to be content with what one has, and the supplementary participle ἐξενεγκών names what he ought to be content with. Chambry sets a space before the Greek question mark.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι μεγίστη παρὰ τοῖς πονηροῖς εὐεργεσίας ἀμοιβὴ τὸ μὴ προσαδικεῖσθαι ὑπ’ αὐτῶν.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti megistē para tois ponērois euergesias amoibē to mē prosadikeisthai hyp’ autōn.
sentences.l: The story shows that with the wicked the greatest return for a good deed is not to be wronged in addition by them.
sentences.n: The articular infinitive τὸ μὴ προσαδικεῖσθαι is the subject: the not-being-further-wronged is itself the return. προσ- adds 'on top of' — the injury laid on top of the kindness. ἀμοιβή is what is given back in exchange, and it answers the μισθός the heron asked for and did not get.
